headline: Rope Bridges Across Amazon Roads Save Thousands of Primates
meta_description: Eight rope bridges installed in Brazil's Amazon enable 15,000 animal crossings over roads, eliminating roadkill at monitored sites and protecting six primate s…
summary_short: Researchers in northern Brazil installed eight rope bridges across forest roads, recording 15,000 crossings by arboreal animals with zero roadkill in 15 months.
body:
Roads fragmenting Brazil's Amazon forests force tree-dwelling primates onto dangerous ground where traffic takes a devastating toll. Researchers have found an elegant solution: rope bridges suspended above traffic. Eight such structures installed in 2024 in Alta Floresta, in northern Mato Grosso state, recorded 15,000 crossings by arboreal animals over the following 15 months—with no roadkill reported at the monitored sites. Six primate species used the bridges, including black-faced black spider monkeys, Schneider's marmosets, and the critically endangered Alta Floresta titi monkey, which has become the symbol of the program.

The bridges are ingeniously designed with multiple rope layers to accommodate different movement styles. Some animals walk across them; others swing by their arms or grip with prehensile tails. Camera footage reveals that adaptation takes time—tufted capuchins needed seven months before attempting their first crossing. The data also shows which designs work best, refined through an earlier project along the BR-174 highway. Over five years, that initiative's 32 bridges recorded about 1,250 primate crossings, helping guide current efforts.

The stakes extend beyond individual safety. Roads don't just endanger animals; they isolate populations and disrupt gene flow—a critical concern for species already confined to small areas. When fruit-eating primates disappear, forests lose seed dispersers essential to regeneration. Brazil's transport infrastructure department has already adopted the Reconecta bridge design as its recommended highway standard, and a national wildlife road-safety plan awaits Senate approval. More bridges are planned across Brazil and into Suriname, though their long-term success depends on maintenance and ongoing monitoring.
quick_facts: Eight bridges installed in Alta Floresta recorded 15,000 animal crossings in 15 months
Six primate species use the structures, including a critically endangered local species
Zero roadkill reported at monitored bridge sites
Multiple rope layers accommodate different animal movement styles
